content: 1. The World Health Organization (WHO) introduced the End TB Strategy in 2015, aiming to eliminate tuberculosis (TB) as a public health threat by 2035. This strategy emphasizes integrated patient-centered care, bold policies, and supportive systems, as well as intensified research and innovation. 2. Uplekar et al. (2015) discussed the WHO's new End TB Strategy in The Lancet, highlighting its focus on reducing TB incidence and mortality through comprehensive approaches, including universal health coverage and social protection. 3. The Stop TB Partnership developed the Global Plan to End TB (2016–2020), which outlines the financial and operational requirements to achieve the targets set by the End TB Strategy. 4. The WHO published a guide titled Implementing the End TB Strategy: The Essentials in 2015, providing countries with practical steps to operationalize the strategy. 5. The WHO's Global Tuberculosis Report 2017 provides a comprehensive overview of the global TB epidemic, including data on incidence, mortality, and progress toward targets. 6. The WHO Global Task Force on TB Impact Measurement monitors and evaluates the impact of TB interventions, ensuring accountability and guiding policy decisions. 7. Boehme et al. (2010) demonstrated the effectiveness of rapid molecular diagnostics for TB and rifampin resistance in the New England Journal of Medicine, emphasizing the importance of early and accurate detection. 8. Diacon et al. (2009) evaluated the efficacy of TMC207 (bedaquiline) for multidrug-resistant TB in a clinical trial published in the New England Journal of Medicine. 9. Gler et al. (2012) reported on the use of delamanid for treating multidrug-resistant pulmonary TB, showing promising results in improving treatment outcomes. 10. The South African Department of Health and the South African National AIDS Council published a summary report in 2016 on the investment case for HIV and TB, emphasizing the economic and health benefits of targeted interventions. 11. Eaton et al. (2014) analyzed the health benefits, costs, and cost-effectiveness of earlier antiretroviral therapy eligibility and expanded treatment coverage using 12 mathematical models, as published in The Lancet Global Health. 12. Pretorius et al. (2014) explored the potential effects of changing HIV treatment policies on TB outcomes in South Africa, using three TB-HIV transmission models. 13. Houben et al. (2016) assessed the feasibility of achieving the 2025 WHO global TB targets in South Africa, China, and India through a combined analysis of 11 mathematical models. 14. Menzies et al. (2016) evaluated the cost-effectiveness and resource implications of aggressive TB control measures in China, India, and South Africa, using nine models. 15. Crown et al. (2017) introduced constrained optimization methods in health services research, providing a framework for resource allocation and decision-making in Value in Health. 16. Briggs et al. (2012) discussed model parameter estimation and uncertainty in health economic modeling, emphasizing best practices for transparency and validation. 17. Siebert et al. (2012) provided guidance on state-transition modeling in health economics, highlighting its application in decision-making processes. 18. Pitman et al. (2012) reviewed dynamic transmission modeling for infectious diseases, emphasizing its role in evaluating intervention strategies. 19. Sullivan et al. (2014) outlined principles of good practice for budget impact analysis, providing a framework for assessing the financial implications of health interventions. 20. Eddy et al. (2012) emphasized the importance of model transparency and validation in health economic evaluations, advocating for standardized reporting practices. 21. Husereau et al. (2013) introduced the Consolidated Health Economic Evaluation Reporting Standards (CHEERS), providing detailed guidance for reporting health economic evaluations. 22. Wilkinson et al. (2016) presented the international decision support initiative reference case for economic evaluation, offering a structured approach to inform health policy decisions. 23. The HIV Modeling Consortium (2015) developed tools and methods to optimize budget allocation for HIV programs, supporting evidence-based decision-making. 24. Delva et al. (2015) explored the impact of expanded HIV treatment programs on prevention, emphasizing the need for optimization to maximize health outcomes. 25. Jit et al. (2011) provided guidance on using cost-effectiveness models for introducing the human papillomavirus (HPV) vaccine in lowand middle-income countries. 26. Jit et al. (2013) published a consensus report on economic analyses to support HPV vaccination decisions in lowand middle-income countries. 27. Shedrawy et al. (2017) discussed methodological considerations for economic modeling of latent TB infection screening in migrants, emphasizing the importance of context-specific approaches.
